mainTopic: בלעם's 'blessing' and prophecies, his evil advice that led ישראל to sin at בעל פעור, and his downfall and death.
overview: This amud starts in the middle of a comparison. אחיה השילוני's 'curse' compared ישראל to a reed, and בלעם's 'blessing' compared them to a cedar. The reed bends with the wind and survives, while the cedar is torn out by one southern wind, so the 'curse' was really better. The גמרא then explains more of בלעם's prophecy. It teaches the fates of פרעה's three advisors, בלעם, איוב, and יתרו, and gives two readings of 'אוי מי יחיה' and a reading of the ships from כתים. Next it describes בלעם's evil advice to בלק: the linen-selling booths, the wine, and the trap that led ישראל to worship בעל פעור. רבי אליעזר and רבי יהושע argue over the meaning of the names שטים, ותקראן, and רפידים. רבי יוחנן teaches that 'וישב' always signals coming trouble. The amud ends with בלעם's death: he came to collect payment for the 24,000 who died, and he fell from נביא to קוסם.

steps.title: The reed bends but survives
steps.stepSummary: The reed (אחיה's 'curse') has a trunk that grows back and many roots. The wind moves it back and forth but never pulls it out, and when the wind stops it stands in its place.
steps.simpleTranslation: [Its trunk] grows back and its roots are many. Even if all the winds in the world blow on it, they can't move it from its place. It just sways back and forth with them, and once the winds calm down, the reed stands in its place again.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its description of the reed, the picture that אחיה השילוני used when he 'cursed' ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reed seems weak because it bends with every wind. But because it bends, and because it has many roots and grows back, it can never be torn out. Its 'weakness' is really what keeps it alive.

keyTerms.meaning: grows back (when cut, a new shoot replaces it)

steps.confusionAlert: This step starts in the middle of a sentence from the previous page. The subject is the reed that אחיה השילוני used to describe ישראל, not the cedar.

phrases.english: [its trunk] grows back, and its roots are many.
phrases.notes: This continues from the previous page. It describes the reed that אחיה השילוני compared ישראל to.

phrases.english: And even if all the winds in the world
come and blow against it,
they do not move it from its place,
rather, it goes back and forth with them.
Once the winds go quiet,
the reed stands in its place.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַחְלִיף, וְשׇׁרָשָׁיו מְרוּבִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the comparison begun on the previous page between אחיה's reed and בלעם's cedar.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The reed survives every wind because it bends, has many roots, and grows back.

steps.title: The cedar looks strong but falls
steps.stepSummary: בלעם blessed ישראל by comparing them to a cedar. The cedar is not near water, has few roots, and does not grow back. Most winds can't move it, but one southern wind tears it out and knocks it flat.
steps.simpleTranslation: But בלעם the wicked blessed them with a cedar. What is a cedar like? It doesn't stand near water, its roots are few, and its trunk doesn't grow back. Even if all the winds in the world blow on it, they can't move it. But once a southern wind blows on it, it immediately pulls it out and turns it over on its face.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now describes the cedar from בלעם's 'blessing' to show that it is weaker than the reed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The cedar never bends, so it looks unbeatable. But it has few roots and cannot grow back, so when the southern wind comes, it is pulled out completely and does not recover. בלעם's 'blessing' hid a curse inside it.

phrases.english: But Bilam the wicked blessed them with a cedar.
phrases.notes: This refers to בלעם's words 'כארזים עלי מים' in במדבר 24:6.

phrases.english: What is a cedar like?
It does not stand in a place of water,
and its roots are few,
and its trunk does not grow back.
Even if all the winds in the world
come and blow against it,
they do not move it from its place.
But once a southern wind blows against it,
it immediately uproots it and turns it over on its face.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל בִּלְעָם הָרָשָׁע בֵּרְכָן בְּאֶרֶז
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts the cedar with the reed described in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The cedar seems strong, but one southern wind destroys it completely.

steps.title: The reed becomes the quill for holy books
steps.stepSummary: There is one more advantage: the reed was chosen to be made into the quill that writes ספרי תורה, נביאים וכתובים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And not only that, but the reed merited to have a quill taken from it to write scrolls of תורה, נביאים, and כתובים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds one more point to show that the reed (אחיה's 'curse') is better than the cedar (בלעם's 'blessing').
steps.deeperAnalysis: Beyond surviving, the reed earns honor: it becomes the pen for all the holy books. This completes the proof that אחיה's 'curse' was better than בלעם's 'blessing'.

keyTerms.meaning: and not only that, but also

steps.whatToRemember: A reed that bends survives and is honored. A proud cedar falls. So the 'curse' of אחיה השילוני is better than the 'blessing' of בלעם.

phrases.english: And not only that, but the reed merited
to have a quill taken from it

phrases.aramaic: לִכְתּוֹב מִמֶּנּוּ סִפְרֵי תוֹרָה, נְבִיאִים וּכְתוּבִים.
phrases.english: to write with it scrolls of Torah, Prophets, and Writings.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֹא עוֹד, אֶלָּא שֶׁזָּכָה קָנֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds an extra advantage of the reed, closing the reed-versus-cedar comparison.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The reed is also honored by becoming the quill for writing holy books.

steps.title: בלעם mocks יתרו the קיני
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a new פסוק about בלעם seeing the קיני. It explains that בלעם was speaking to יתרו and asking how he ended up among the strong ones of the world when he had been part of the same plan.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And he saw the קיני and took up his parable.' בלעם said to יתרו: 'קיני, weren't you with us in that plan? Who seated you next to the mighty ones of the world?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic, explaining a פסוק where בלעם speaks to the קיני, whom it identifies as יתרו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בלעם reminds יתרו that they were both advisors in the same plan. He asks, almost jealously, how יתרו came to sit among ישראל, 'the mighty of the world,' while בלעם did not. The next step explains what that plan was and why יתרו ended up differently.

keyTerms.meaning: the קיני, a name for יתרו
the mighty, firm ones of the world

phrases.english: "And he saw the Kenite and took up his parable."
phrases.notes: במדבר 24:21

phrases.english: Bilam said to Yisro:

phrases.aramaic: קֵינִי, לֹא הָיִיתָ עִמָּנוּ בְּאוֹתָהּ עֵצָה?
phrases.english: Kenite, weren't you with us in that plan?
phrases.notes: This is the plan in פרעה's court to drown the Jewish baby boys.

phrases.english: Who seated you next to the mighty ones of the world?
phrases.notes: This plays on the next words of the פסוק, 'איתן מושבך,' 'firm is your dwelling.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וַיַּרְא אֶת הַקֵּינִי וַיִּשָּׂא מְשָׁלוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next part of בלעם's speech, a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בלעם's words to the קיני are read as a jab at יתרו, who had been with him in פרעה's plan.

steps.title: The three advisors of פרעה and their fates
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports the idea with רבי סימאי's teaching. Three people were in פרעה's plan: בלעם, איוב, and יתרו. בלעם, who gave the advice, was killed. איוב, who stayed silent, suffered. יתרו, who ran away, had descendants who sat in לשכת הגזית.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי סימאי: Three were in that plan: בלעם, איוב, and יתרו. בלעם, who advised, was killed. איוב, who was silent, was punished with suffering. And יתרו, who ran away, earned that his descendants sat in לשכת הגזית.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that בלעם's words in step 4 match a known teaching about the three people in פרעה's plan.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each person's fate matches how he acted. Advising evil led to death, silence led to suffering, and running away from evil led to great honor for one's family. This explains why יתרו was 'seated among the mighty.'

keyTerms.meaning: and this is what [so-and-so] said, an introduction to a supporting teaching
the Chamber of Hewn Stone, where the סנהדרין sat

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a classic teaching that staying silent while evil is planned is itself punished, and that fleeing from evil brings great reward.

phrases.aramaic: וְהַיְינוּ דְּאָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא
phrases.english: And this is what Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said
that Rabbi Simai said:
Three were in that plan,
and these are they: Bilam, Iyov, and Yisro.
Bilam, who advised, was killed;
Iyov, who was silent, was punished with suffering;
and Yisro, who ran away,

phrases.aramaic: זָכוּ בְּנֵי בָנָיו לֵישֵׁב בְּלִשְׁכַּת הַגָּזִית,
phrases.english: his descendants merited to sit in the Chamber of Hewn Stone,

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַיְינוּ דְּאָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי סִימַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Backs up step 4 by showing that יתרו really was in that plan and was later rewarded.
steps.raayaObject: That יתרו was part of פרעה's plan yet ended up honored among ישראל.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי סימאי's teaching, quoted by רבי חייא בר אבא, about the three advisors.

steps.title: Proof that יתרו's descendants were scribes
steps.stepSummary: Two פסוקים prove the reward. One says the families of scribes were the קינים. The other says the קיני was משה's father-in-law, which is יתרו.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'And the families of scribes who lived in יעבץ: the תרעתים, שמעתים, and שוכתים. They are the קינים who came from חמת, father of the house of רכב.' And it says: 'And the children of the קיני, משה's father-in-law, went up from the city of palm trees.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא proves from פסוקים that יתרו's descendants became the scribes who sat in לשכת הגזית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first פסוק shows that the scribes were 'קינים.' The second פסוק shows that the 'קיני' means the family of משה's father-in-law, יתרו. Put together, the scribes were יתרו's descendants.

keyTerms.meaning: as it says, introducing a פסוק as proof

steps.whatToRemember: בלעם advised and was killed, איוב was silent and suffered, and יתרו fled and earned that his descendants became scribes of the סנהדרין. Two פסוקים connect those scribes to יתרו.

phrases.english: as it says: "And the families of scribes who lived in Yabetz:
phrases.notes: דברי הימים א 2:55

phrases.english: the Tirathites, Shimeathites, and Sucathites;
they are the Kenites who came
from Chamat, father of the house of Rechav."
And it is written: "And the children of the Kenite, Moshe's father-in-law,
phrases.notes: שופטים 1:16. This shows that 'the Kenites' are יתרו's family.

phrases.english: went up from the city of palm trees."

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: וּמִשְׁפְּחוֹת סוֹפְרִים יוֹשְׁבֵי יַעְבֵּץ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the scriptural source for יתרו's reward stated in step 5.
steps.raayaObject: That יתרו's descendants sat as scribes in לשכת הגזית.
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברי הימים א 2:55 combined with שופטים 1:16.

steps.title: Woe to the one who lives off God's name
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes בלעם's cry 'אוי מי יחיה משמו אל.' ריש לקיש reads it as בלעם mourning himself, a man who made his living by using God's name.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'He took up his parable and said: Alas, who shall live from God's name?' ריש לקיש says this means: Woe to the person who keeps himself alive by using God's name.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new פסוק from בלעם's prophecy. ריש לקיש explains what the strange words mean.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש reads 'משמו אל' as 'from God's name.' So the 'אוי' is about someone who earns his living by speaking in God's name, which is exactly what בלעם did. In this reading, בלעם is really describing himself.

keyTerms.meaning: keeps himself alive, makes his living

phrases.english: "And he took up his parable, and said:
Alas, who shall live from what God has appointed?"
phrases.notes: במדבר 24:23

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says:

phrases.aramaic: אוֹי מִי שֶׁמְּחַיֶּה עַצְמוֹ בְּשֵׁם אֵל.
phrases.english: Woe to the one who keeps himself alive by the name of God.
phrases.notes: He reads משמו as 'from His name.' בלעם made his living speaking in God's name.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַיִּשָּׂא מְשָׁלוֹ וַיֹּאמַר אוֹי מִי יִחְיֶה מִשֻּׂמוֹ אֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the קיני (יתרו) to the next פסוק in בלעם's prophecy.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ריש לקיש: the פסוק is a woe on one who makes his living through God's name, meaning בלעם himself.

steps.title: Woe to the nation that blocks God's redemption
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן reads the same פסוק differently. It is a woe on any nation that gets in the way when God redeems ישראל, like someone who throws his cloak between two mating lions.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן says: Woe to the nation that is found standing in the way when the הקב"ה redeems His children. Who would throw his garment between a lion and a lioness while they are mating?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives a second explanation of the same 'אוי' פסוק. He uses a word picture to show how dangerous it is to interfere.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For ריש לקיש the woe was about בלעם himself. For רבי יוחנן it is about the nations at the time of the redemption. Coming between God and His children is as deadly as stepping between two lions while they mate.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan says:
Woe to the nation that will be found

phrases.aramaic: בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹשֶׂה פִּדְיוֹן לְבָנָיו.
phrases.english: at the time when the Holy One, Blessed be He, redeems His children.

phrases.aramaic: מִי מֵטִיל כְּסוּתוֹ בֵּין לָבִיא לִלְבִיאָה
phrases.english: Who throws his garment between a lion and a lioness
at the time when they are mating with each other?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: אוֹי לָהּ לָאוּמָּה שֶׁתִּמָּצֵא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second reading of the same פסוק, different from ריש לקיש's.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יוחנן: the פסוק is a woe on the nation that interferes when God redeems ישראל.

steps.title: The ships from כתים are a Roman army
steps.stepSummary: On the פסוק 'וצים מיד כתים,' רב explains that the ships are a Roman legion.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'And ships come from the coast of כתים.' רב says: this is the Roman legion.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next פסוק in בלעם's prophecy. רב tells us who these ships are.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק only mentions ships from a far coast. רב identifies them as a Roman army unit, the force that will come and attack אשור.

phrases.english: "And ships come from the coast of Kittim"
phrases.notes: במדבר 24:24

phrases.english: Rav says: This is the Roman legion.
phrases.notes: ליבון אספיר is a foreign phrase for a Roman army unit.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְצִים מִיַּד כִּתִּים, אָמַר רַב: לִיבּוֹן אַסְפִּיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues to the next פסוק in בלעם's prophecy.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: the ships from כתים are the Roman legion.

steps.title: Killing until אשור, enslaving afterward
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the rest of the פסוק, 'ועינו אשור ועינו עבר.' Until אשור, the enemies kill ישראל. From then on they only enslave them.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And they shall afflict אשור, and they shall afflict עבר.' Until אשור, they kill. From then on, they enslave.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes explaining the same פסוק about כתים. It shows that the enemies' treatment of ישראל changes over time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'ועינו' (afflict) appears twice, once for אשור and once for עבר. The גמרא splits history into two stages. Before אשור, the enemies kill, and after that point they enslave instead of killing.

keyTerms.meaning: עבר, here meaning the Jewish people

phrases.english: "And they shall afflict Assyria, and they shall afflict Eber" –
phrases.notes: במדבר 24:24

phrases.english: until Assyria, they kill outright;
phrases.notes: The ones being killed and later enslaved are the Jewish people.

phrases.english: from that point on, they enslave them.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעִנּוּ אַשּׁוּר וְעִנּוּ עֵבֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the explanation of the same פסוק begun in step 9.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Before אשור the enemies kill ישראל; afterward they only enslave them.

steps.title: Why did בלעם reverse the wording?
steps.stepSummary: בלעם tells בלק he will advise him 'what this people will do to your people.' The גמרא asks why. It should have said what YOUR people (מואב) will do to THIS people (ישראל), since בלעם's advice was about harming ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: בלעם said: 'I am going to my people. Come, I will advise you what this people will do to your people.' But he should have said 'your people to this people'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a פסוק and points out that its wording seems backwards. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בלעם was giving בלק a plan to hurt ישראל. So logically it should read 'what your people will do to this people.' The פסוק says the opposite, and the גמרא wants to know why.

phrases.english: "Behold, I go to my people;
come, and I shall advise you
what this people shall do to your people."
phrases.notes: במדבר 24:14

phrases.english: He should have said: "your people to this people"!

steps.triggerLanguage: עַמְּךָ לְעָם הַזֶּה מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns to a new פסוק about בלעם's advice to בלק.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: בלעם's advice was for מואב to harm ישראל, so the order of the words seems backwards.

steps.title: Saying a curse about someone else
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא בר כהנא answers: בלעם spoke like a person who means to curse himself but pins the curse on others. He did not want to say out loud that ישראל would be harmed, so he flipped it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא בר כהנא says: It is like a person who curses himself but hangs the curse on other people.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא בר כהנא answers the question about the backwards wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The real meaning was 'your people will harm this people (ישראל).' Saying something bad about ישראל directly was too harsh, so בלעם turned the words around. People do the same when they avoid saying a bad thing about themselves and say it about others instead.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba bar Kahana says:
It is like a person who curses himself
and hangs his curse on others.
phrases.notes: He doesn't want to say the bad thing about himself out loud, so he says it about someone else.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בַּר כָּהֲנָא: כְּאָדָם שֶׁמְּקַלֵּל אֶת עַצְמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The wording was flipped on purpose, to avoid saying a curse directly.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The wording looked backwards, as if ישראל would harm מואב.
steps.terutzMaskana: The real meaning is that מואב will harm ישראל, but it is phrased about the other side.
steps.whatToRemember: The פסוק means 'your people will do to this people.' בלעם turned it around so as not to say the harm openly.

steps.title: בלעם's plan: linen and immorality
steps.stepSummary: בלעם explains his plan. ישראל's God hates immorality, and ישראל wants linen clothing. So set up tent booths with prostitutes, an old woman outside and a young woman inside, selling linen garments.
steps.simpleTranslation: בלעם said to them: The God of these people hates immorality, and they want linen clothes. Come, I'll give you advice. Make curtain booths for them and put prostitutes inside, an old woman outside and a young woman inside, and have them sell linen garments.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts telling the actual evil advice בלעם gave. It explains how the trap was set up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בלעם could not curse ישראל, so he looked for a way to make God angry at them. He used two facts: God hates immorality, and ישראל wanted linen. The linen was the bait to draw them into the booths.

keyTerms.meaning: and I will give you advice

phrases.english: He said to them:

phrases.aramaic: אֱלֹהֵיהֶם שֶׁל אֵלּוּ שׂוֹנֵא זִימָּה הוּא,
phrases.english: The God of these people hates immorality,
and they crave linen garments.
Come, and I will give you advice:
Make for them enclosures of hangings,
and seat prostitutes in them,
an old woman outside and a young woman inside,
and let them sell them linen garments.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶם: אֱלֹהֵיהֶם שֶׁל אֵלּוּ שׂוֹנֵא זִימָּה הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the advice ('איעצך') that the פסוק in step 11 mentioned.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בלעם's advice: use linen as bait to draw ישראל into immorality, which their God hates.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains how בלעם, who could not curse ישראל, still managed to harm them by leading them into sin.

steps.title: The booths are set up and the bargain prices draw people in
steps.stepSummary: בלעם's plan is put into action. Curtained booths are set up along a long stretch of land, each with an old woman outside and a young woman inside. They lure Jews in with linen at fair and then cheaper prices, again and again.
steps.simpleTranslation: He made curtained booths for them from the Snow Mountain until בית הישימות, and placed prostitutes in them, an old woman outside and a young woman inside. When ישראל were eating, drinking, happy, and strolling in the market, the old woman would ask a Jew: 'Aren't you looking for linen clothes?' The old woman would quote the fair price, and the young woman would quote a lower price. This happened two or three times.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now tells how the plan from Step 13 actually played out. This is the first stage of the trap: winning trust with good deals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The old woman outside looks harmless and draws people in. Inside, the young woman offers an even better price, so the Jew comes back again and again. The repeat visits slowly build trust.

keyTerms.meaning: Curtains or hangings used to make enclosures, here tent booths
At the fair price, what it is worth

phrases.english: He made curtained enclosures for them
phrases.notes: This is בלק putting בלעם's advice into action.

phrases.english: from the Snow Mountain until Beit HaYeshimot,
and he placed prostitutes in them,
an old woman outside and a young woman inside.
And when the Jews would eat and drink
and be happy and go out to stroll in the market,
the old woman would say to him:
Aren't you looking for linen clothes?
The old woman would quote him the fair price,
and the young woman would quote him less,
two and three times.

steps.triggerLanguage: עָשָׂה לָהֶן קְלָעִים מֵהַר שֶׁלֶג עַד בֵּית הַיְשִׁימוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Carries out the plan בלעם described in Step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The trap began with friendly, cheap sales that built trust over repeated visits.

steps.title: Friendliness and wine break down his guard
steps.stepSummary: After several visits, the young woman treats the Jew like family and offers him wine. The wine was not yet forbidden. Once he drinks, his desire flares up.
steps.simpleTranslation: Afterward she would say to him: 'You are like one of the family, sit and choose for yourself.' A jug of Ammonite wine sat next to her. At that time neither Ammonite wine nor gentile wine had been forbidden yet. She said to him: 'Would you like a cup of wine?' Once he drank, his desire burned inside him.
steps.whatsHappening: The trap moves to its second stage: closeness and wine. The גמרא adds that drinking this wine was not yet forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First came trust, now comes comfort. The wine weakens his self-control. The side remark that the wine was still allowed shows that the slide began with something technically permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: Like a member of the household, like family
It burned in him, meaning his desire flared up

steps.confusionAlert: The line about the wine not being forbidden yet is not saying he did nothing wrong. It only says this first step was still allowed at the time. The real sins come next.

phrases.english: And afterward she would say to him:
You are like one of the family,
sit and choose for yourself.

phrases.aramaic: וְצַרְצוּרי שֶׁל יַיִן עַמּוֹנִי מוּנָּח אֶצְלָהּ,
phrases.english: And a jug of Ammonite wine was placed beside her,

phrases.aramaic: וַעֲדַיִין לֹא נֶאֱסַר יַיִן שֶׁל עַמּוֹנִי
phrases.english: and Ammonite wine had not yet been forbidden,
nor the wine of gentiles.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרָה לוֹ: רְצוֹנֶךָ שֶׁתִּשְׁתֶּה כּוֹס שֶׁל יַיִן?
phrases.english: She said to him: Would you like to drink a cup of wine?
Once he drank, it burned within him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַחַר כָּךְ אוֹמֶרֶת לוֹ: הֲרֵי אַתְּ כְּבֶן בַּיִת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The next stage of the same trap, after trust was built in Step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Comfort and wine, which was not yet forbidden, broke down the Jew's self-control.

steps.title: The demand to worship פעור and deny the Torah
steps.stepSummary: When he asks her to be with him, she pulls out her idol and tells him to worship it first. She plays it down as just uncovering himself, which is in fact how פעור is worshipped. Then she demands that he deny the Torah. A פסוק in הושע is brought as support.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to her: 'Give in to me.' She took her idol out of her bosom and said: 'Worship this!' He said: 'Am I not a Jew?' She said: 'What do you care? We are only asking you to uncover yourself.' But he did not know that this is exactly how it is worshipped. 'And more than that, I will not let you go until you deny the Torah of משה your teacher.' As the פסוק says: 'They came to בעל פעור and gave themselves over to shame, and they became disgusting like the thing they loved.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is the last stage of the trap. Desire is used to push the Jew into עבודה זרה and then into denying the Torah itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He still knows a Jew may not worship idols, so she makes the act sound small and meaningless. But פיעור is the actual way פעור is worshipped, so he worships it without realizing. The פסוק shows that ישראל gave themselves over to the 'shame' of פעור.

keyTerms.meaning: Give in to me, listen to my request
Literally 'the thing she feared/revered', meaning her idol
Uncovering oneself to relieve oneself, the way פעור was worshipped

steps.whatToRemember: בלעם's plan worked in small steps: cheap prices, then friendliness, then wine, then desire, then idol worship, and finally denying the whole Torah.
steps.whyThisMatters: This explains how ישראל fell at בעל פעור. It also shows why בלעם's advice was so dangerous, as Steps 11–13 set up.

phrases.english: He said to her: Give in to me.
She took out her idol from her bosom,
phrases.notes: יראתה literally means 'the thing she reveres', so it is her idol.

phrases.english: and said to him: Worship this!
He said to her: Am I not a Jew?
She said to him: And what do you care?
Are we asking anything of you except to uncover yourself?
phrases.notes: פיעור means exposing yourself to relieve yourself.

phrases.english: [But he does not know that this is how it is worshipped.]
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets are the corrected wording. He was worshipping פעור without even realizing it.

phrases.english: And not only that, but I will not let you go
until you deny the Torah of Moshe your teacher,
as it is said:
"They came to Baal Peor
phrases.notes: הושע 9:10

phrases.english: and dedicated themselves to the shameful thing
and became detestable like what they loved."

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לָהּ: הִשָּׁמֵיעִי לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The final stage of the trap: the desire from Step 15 is used to bring him to idol worship and denying the Torah.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Desire was used to drag the Jew into worshipping פעור, made to look trivial, and then into denying the Torah, as the פסוק in הושע describes.

steps.title: What does the name שטים mean?
steps.stepSummary: On the פסוק 'וישב ישראל בשטים', רבי אליעזר says שטים is simply the name of the place. רבי יהושע says the name hints that ישראל got busy with foolishness (שטות).
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And ישראל settled in שטים.' רבי אליעזר says: שטים is the place's name. רבי יהושע says: it means they busied themselves with matters of foolishness.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to the פסוק that opens the פעור story and brings a מחלוקת about the word שטים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר reads the word plainly, as a place name. רבי יהושע reads it as a hint, because שטים sounds like שטות, foolishness. That fits the sins just described.

keyTerms.meaning: The place where ישראל camped before the פעור sin

phrases.english: "And Israel dwelt in Shittim."
phrases.notes: במדבר 25:1

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer says: Shittim is its name.
Rabbi Yehoshua says:
That they busied themselves with matters of foolishness.
phrases.notes: A wordplay: שטים sounds like שטות.

steps.triggerLanguage: וַיֵּשֶׁב יִשְׂרָאֵל בַּשִּׁטִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the story of the trap to explaining the פסוק that opens the פעור episode.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אליעזר: שטים is a plain place name. רבי יהושע: it hints at their foolish, sinful behavior.

steps.title: What does 'they called the people' mean?
steps.stepSummary: On the פסוק 'ותקראן לעם לזבחי אלהיהן', רבי אליעזר says naked women met them. רבי יהושע says they all became בעלי קריין.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says 'And they called the people to the sacrifices of their gods.' רבי אליעזר says: naked women came out to meet them. רבי יהושע says: they all became people who had a seminal emission.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next פסוק in the story and brings two readings of the word 'ותקראן'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר hears 'ותקראן' as meeting: the women came out to meet the men. רבי יהושע hears in it the word קרי: the men were so overcome by desire that they all became impure. Either way, the word shows how far the men fell.

keyTerms.meaning: People who had a seminal emission

phrases.english: "And they called the people to the sacrifices of their gods"
phrases.notes: במדבר 25:2

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר: עֲרוּמּוֹת פָּגְעוּ בָּהֶן.
phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer says: naked women met them.
phrases.notes: He hears ותקראן as coming from 'meeting' (like לקראת).

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua says:
that they all became people who had a seminal emission.
phrases.notes: He hears ותקראן as coming from the word קרי.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר: עֲרוּמּוֹת פָּגְעוּ בָּהֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same pair of תנאים, now reading the next פסוק of the שטים story (במדבר 25:2).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אליעזר: naked women met them. רבי יהושע: they all became בעלי קריין.

steps.title: What does the name רפידים mean?
steps.stepSummary: Because רבי אליעזר and רבי יהושע argued about place names, the גמרא asks about another place name: רפידים.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the meaning of the word 'רפידים'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up the next move. It asks about the place name רפידים, because just before this the same תנאים argued about the name שטים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This question is not about the שטים story at all. It is a side topic that fits the pattern from step 17: one view says a place name is just a name, and the other finds a hint in it.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the meaning of the word
רפידים, a place where ישראל camped (שמות 19:2)

phrases.english: What is the meaning of the word "Rephidim"?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי לְשׁוֹן ״רְפִידִים״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side question, sparked by the argument over the name שטים in step 17.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the name רפידים carries a hidden meaning.

steps.title: רפידים: just a name, or slacking off from תורה?
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר says רפידים is simply the name of the place. רבי יהושע says it hints that ישראל slackened (ריפו) in Torah, and he proves it from a פסוק in ירמיהו.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר says: רפידים is its name. רבי יהושע says: it hints that they let themselves go slack in Torah, as it says, 'Fathers do not turn back to their children because of weakness (רפיון) of hands.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with the same kind of argument as for שטים: is it just a name, or does it carry a message?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהושע connects רפידים to the word רפיון, meaning weakness. The פסוק in ירמיהו shows that 'רפיון ידים' means weakness, so for him the place name teaches that ישראל grew weak in their Torah learning there.

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer says: Rephidim is its name.
Rabbi Yehoshua says:
that they let themselves go slack in words of Torah,
as it is said: "Fathers do not turn back to their children
because of weakness of hands."
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 47:3

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר אוֹמֵר: רְפִידִים שְׁמָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבי אליעזר: just a name. רבי יהושע: it hints at weakening in Torah, based on 'רפיון ידים'.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: 'and he dwelt' always signals trouble
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן teaches that wherever the פסוק says 'וישב', it is a sign of pain. His first proof is 'וישב ישראל בשטים', which is followed by the sin with the daughters of מואב.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: Wherever it says 'וישב' (and he dwelt), it means trouble. As it says: 'And ישראל dwelt in שטים, and the people began to act immorally with the daughters of מואב.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives a general rule about the word 'וישב' and starts proving it from our story in שטים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Settling down sounds peaceful, but רבי יוחנן says that in the תנ״ך it comes right before trouble. In שטים, the very same פסוק that says ישראל settled also says they began to sin.

keyTerms.meaning: A word that signals pain or trouble

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
Every place where it says "and he dwelt"
it is nothing but a word of pain,
as it is said: "And Israel dwelt in Shittim

phrases.aramaic: וַיָּחֶל הָעָם לִזְנוֹת אֶל בְּנוֹת מוֹאָב״.
phrases.english: and the people began to act immorally with the daughters of Moab."
phrases.notes: במדבר 25:1

steps.triggerLanguage: כׇּל מָקוֹם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וַיֵּשֶׁב״ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא לְשׁוֹן צַעַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the פסוק 'וישב ישראל בשטים' (step 17) and draws a general rule from it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Every 'וישב' in the תנ״ך signals coming trouble.

steps.title: More proofs: יעקב, ישראל in גושן, and the days of שלמה
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן shows three more times that 'וישב' is followed by trouble: יעקב settles and then יוסף brings a bad report, ישראל settles in גושן and then יעקב is close to death, and יהודה and ישראל dwell safely and then an enemy rises against שלמה.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And יעקב dwelt in the land where his father had lived, in the land of כנען', and then 'יוסף brought a bad report about them to their father.' And it says: 'And ישראל dwelt in the land of גושן', and then 'The days of ישראל drew near to die.' 'And יהודה and ישראל dwelt safely, each man under his vine and under his fig tree', and then 'ה׳ raised up an enemy against שלמה, הדד the אדומי, from the king's family in אדום.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן backs up his rule with three more pairs of פסוקים. Each pair shows a 'וישב' and then the trouble that came after it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proofs come in pairs: the first פסוק has 'וישב', and the second shows the trouble. They cover very different times, from the אבות through the days of שלמה, which shows the rule holds everywhere.

keyTerms.meaning: הדד from אדום, an enemy of שלמה

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן's rule: when the תנ״ך says someone 'settled down' (וישב), expect trouble to follow.

phrases.english: "And Jacob dwelt in the land where his father had lived
in the land of Canaan,"
phrases.notes: בראשית 37:1

phrases.aramaic: ״וַיָּבֵא יוֹסֵף אֶת דִּבָּתָם רָעָה אֶל אֲבִיהֶם״.
phrases.english: "And Joseph brought a bad report about them to their father."
phrases.notes: בראשית 37:2. This is the trouble that came right after יעקב settled.

phrases.english: And it is said: "And Israel dwelt in the land of Goshen,"
"And the days of Israel drew near to die."
"And Judah and Israel dwelt safely,
each man under his vine and under his fig tree,"
phrases.notes: מלכים א 5:5

phrases.english: "And God raised up an enemy against Solomon,
Hadad the Edomite;
he was from the king's family in Edom."
phrases.notes: מלכים א 11:14

steps.triggerLanguage: ״וַיֵּשֶׁב יַעֲקֹב בְּאֶרֶץ מְגוּרֵי אָבִיו בְּאֶרֶץ כְּנָעַן״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds more proofs for רבי יוחנן's rule from step 21.

steps.title: Why was בלעם in the war with מדין?
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק says בלעם was killed by the sword together with the kings of מדין. The גמרא asks what he was doing there.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And they killed the kings of מדין along with their other slain, and they killed בלעם son of בעור with the sword.' What was בלעם doing there?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to בלעם and asks why he was present at the war against מדין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בלעם was not a king of מדין and did not live there, so it is strange that he died in their war. The question sets up רבי יוחנן's answer in the next step.

phrases.aramaic: ״וְאֶת מַלְכֵי מִדְיָן הָרְגוּ עַל חַלְלֵיהֶם וְגוֹ׳
phrases.english: "And the kings of Midian they killed along with their slain, etc.

phrases.aramaic: וְאֶת בִּלְעָם בֶּן בְּעוֹר הָרְגוּ בֶּחָרֶב״.
phrases.english: and Balaam son of Beor they killed with the sword."
phrases.notes: במדבר 31:8

phrases.english: Balaam, what was he doing there?

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּלְעָם מַאי בָּעֵי הָתָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the 'וישב' topic and goes back to בלעם, whose plan was told in steps 13-16.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why בלעם was present at the war of מדין.

steps.title: בלעם came to collect his fee
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן answers that בלעם went to collect payment for the 24,000 Jews who died because of his advice.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: He went to collect payment for the twenty-four thousand Jews he had brought down.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers the question: בלעם came to מדין to get paid for his evil plan.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 24,000 who died in the plague after the sin at פעור died because of בלעם's plan. He came to collect his reward for that, and instead he was killed.

keyTerms.meaning: That he brought down, caused to fall

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
That he went to collect payment
for the twenty-four thousand [of Israel that he brought down].
phrases.notes: These are the 24,000 who died in the plague (במדבר 25:9). The words in square brackets are the corrected wording.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁהָלַךְ לִיטּוֹל שְׂכַר עֶשְׂרִים וְאַרְבָּעָה אֶלֶף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: בלעם went to מדין to collect payment for the 24,000 who died through his advice.

steps.title: The camel that lost its ears
steps.stepSummary: רב compares בלעם to the folk saying about a camel that went looking for horns and had its ears cut off.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא בר טוביה said in the name of רב: This is what people say: The camel went to ask for horns, and the ears it had were cut off.
steps.whatsHappening: רב adds a popular saying that sums up what happened to בלעם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The camel wanted something extra (horns) and lost what it already had (its ears). In the same way, בלעם went to get a reward, and instead of gaining anything he lost his life.
steps.whatToRemember: בלעם came to collect a reward for causing ישראל's downfall, and instead he lost his life, like the camel that wanted horns and lost its ears.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר מָר זוּטְרָא בַּר טוֹבִיָּה אָמַר רַב,
phrases.english: Mar Zutra bar Toviya said in the name of Rav:
This is what people say:
The camel went to ask for horns,
and the ears it had were cut off from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַיְינוּ דְּאָמְרִי אִינָשֵׁי: גַּמְלָא אֲזַלָא לְמִיבְעֵי קַרְנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sums up רבי יוחנן's answer in step 24 with a popular saying.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בלעם sought a reward and lost his life, like the camel that sought horns and lost its ears.

steps.title: Why is בלעם called a diviner if he was a prophet?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the פסוק that calls בלעם 'the קוסם' and objects that he was actually a נביא.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'And בלעם son of בעור, the diviner.' A diviner? He is a prophet!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a פסוק about בלעם and points out that the word it uses for him does not seem to fit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קוסם uses lower, impure methods to try to see the future. A נביא receives real messages from הקב"ה, and the תורה shows that בלעם did receive such messages. So the גמרא asks why the פסוק calls him by the lower title.

keyTerms.meaning: Diviner: someone who uses magic-like methods to predict things
Prophet: someone who receives messages from הקב"ה
בלעם son of בעור, the non-Jewish prophet who tried to curse ישראל

phrases.english: "And Balaam son of Beor, the diviner."
phrases.notes: יהושע 13:22. It's a different פסוק from the one in step 23 (במדבר 31:8), but it also tells of בלעם being killed by the sword.

phrases.english: A diviner? He is a prophet!

steps.triggerLanguage: קוֹסֵם? נָבִיא הוּא!
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a second פסוק about בלעם's death (יהושע 13:22, not the במדבר 31:8 of step 23) and looks closely at the title it gives him.
steps.kashyaTarget: The פסוק's description of בלעם as a קוסם.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: בלעם clearly received prophecy, so calling him only a diviner seems wrong.

steps.title: He started as a prophet and ended as a diviner
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן answers that בלעם was a נביא at first, but by the end he had sunk to being just a קוסם.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: At first he was a prophet, and in the end he was a diviner.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers the question by explaining that both titles are true, just at different times in בלעם's life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is no contradiction: earlier פסוקים describe him when he still had prophecy. By the time he was killed, he had lost it and was only a קוסם, so the פסוק in יהושע describes him as he was at his death.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
At first a prophet, and in the end a diviner.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: בַּתְּחִלָּה נָבִיא, וּלְבַסּוֹף קוֹסֵם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting by time: each title fits a different stage of his life.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It seemed the פסוק was contradicting the fact that he was a נביא.
steps.terutzMaskana: He lost his prophecy, so at his death he was only a קוסם.

steps.title: A folk saying about falling from greatness
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא compares בלעם's fall to a saying about a woman from a noble family who disgraced herself with carpenters.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: This is what people say: She came from princes and rulers, and she was promiscuous with carpenters.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא adds a popular saying that captures רבי יוחנן's point about בלעם's fall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The saying describes someone who started at the very top and sank to the very bottom. That matches בלעם: he went from the high level of נבואה down to the low level of a קוסם. Like the camel saying in step 25, this is another folk comparison about בלעם.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what people say, introducing a folk saying

steps.whatToRemember: בלעם had real נבואה but lost it. The פסוק calls him a קוסם because that is what he had become by the end, and רב פפא's saying shows how far he fell.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
This is what people say:
She was from princes and rulers,
phrases.notes: This saying is about a woman.

phrases.english: yet she was promiscuous with carpenters.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא הַיְינוּ דְּאָמְרִי אִינָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates רבי יוחנן's answer with a folk saying.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בלעם's fall from נביא to קוסם is like a noblewoman who sank to disgrace with lowly workmen.
